decks.title: Mid-Point and Intercept Theorems — Part 1: The mid-point theorem
goals: State the mid-point theorem and prove it using congruent triangles
Use it to find lengths and angles and to show lines are parallel
Find the perimeter of the triangle formed by joining mid-points
Show that the mid-points of the sides of any quadrilateral form a parallelogram and name the special cases

slides.heading: Mid-point and intercept theorems, Part 1
slides.body_md: Join the **mid-points** of two sides of a triangle. The new segment is **parallel to the third side and half as long**.

visual.alt: Triangle A B C with D the mid-point of A B and E the mid-point of A C. Equal tick marks show A D equals D B and A E equals E C. The segment D E has the same parallel arrow mark as B C, so D E is parallel to B C.
visual.caption: D and E are mid-points: D E is parallel to B C and half as long.

slides.narration: Welcome. In this chapter we study a small but powerful idea. Take a triangle and join the mid-points of two of its sides. The new segment is parallel to the third side, and exactly half as long. In this first part we prove it, use it to find lengths and angles, and see what it says about shapes made by joining mid-points.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: **State and prove** the mid-point theorem
Find **lengths and angles** with it
Show that lines are **parallel**
Use the **triangle of mid-points**: perimeter is half
Show the **quadrilateral of mid-points** is a parallelogram

rows: joins of two mid-points: parallel to the third side, half as long
its perimeter is half the perimeter of the triangle
always a parallelogram; its sides are half the diagonals

visual.alt: Table of the three results of part one: the mid-point theorem, the triangle of mid-points and the quadrilateral of mid-points.

slides.narration: By the end of this part you will be able to state and prove the mid-point theorem, find lengths and angles with it, and show that lines are parallel. You will also see two shapes made by joining mid-points: the triangle of mid-points, whose perimeter is half, and the quadrilateral of mid-points, which is always a parallelogram.

slides.heading: Tools we will use
slides.body_md: The proof needs five ideas from earlier geometry.

rows: two triangles are congruent: all matching parts are equal
angles across a crossing point are equal
lines are parallel exactly when these angles are equal
one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel makes a parallelogram
a point that cuts a segment into two equal halves

visual.alt: Table of five tools used in the proofs: side angle side congruence, vertically opposite angles, alternate and corresponding angles, the parallelogram test and the idea of a mid-point.

slides.narration: The proof needs five ideas you already know. Triangles that match in side, angle, side are congruent. Vertically opposite angles are equal. Alternate and corresponding angles tell us when lines are parallel. One pair of opposite sides, equal and parallel, makes a parallelogram. And a mid-point cuts a segment into two equal halves.

slides.heading: The mid-point theorem
slides.body_md:
**Theorem.** The segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is **parallel** to the third side and **equal to half** of it.

In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$, so $DE \parallel BC$ and $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$.

visual.alt: Triangle A B C with B C eight centimetres. D and E are the mid-points of A B and A C and D E measures four centimetres, half of B C, and is parallel to it.
visual.caption: Drawn to scale: B C is 8 cm and D E is 4 cm.

slides.narration: Here is the theorem. In triangle A B C, D is the mid-point of A B and E is the mid-point of A C. Then D E is parallel to B C, and D E is half of B C. In the drawing B C is eight centimetres and D E is four centimetres. The tick marks show the equal halves, and the arrows show the parallel lines.

slides.heading: Proof, step 1: the construction
slides.body_md:
Given: $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$.

**Construction.** Produce $DE$ to $F$ so that $EF = DE$, and join $CF$.

visual.alt: The proof figure. Triangle A B C has D and E the mid-points of A B and A C. D E is produced to F so that E F equals D E, and C F is joined. Triangles A E D and C E F are shaded and have equal tick marks on their matching sides.
visual.caption: Construction: produce D E to F so that E F = D E, then join C F.

slides.narration: Now the proof. We are given that D and E are the mid-points of A B and A C. We build a helper point. Extend the line D E beyond E to a point F so that E F equals D E. Then join C to F. The dashed line is the new segment. The idea is to make two triangles that match.

slides.heading: Proof, step 2: two congruent triangles
slides.body_md: Compare $\triangle AED$ and $\triangle CEF$ (shaded).
bullets: $AE = EC$ because $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$
$DE = EF$ by the construction
$\angle AED = \angle CEF$, vertically opposite angles
So $\triangle AED \cong \triangle CEF$ (side angle side)

visual.alt: The proof figure. Triangle A B C has D and E the mid-points of A B and A C. D E is produced to F so that E F equals D E, and C F is joined. Triangles A E D and C E F are shaded and have equal tick marks on their matching sides.
visual.caption: Construction: produce D E to F so that E F = D E, then join C F.

slides.narration: Compare the two shaded triangles, A E D and C E F. A E equals E C, because E is the mid-point of A C. D E equals E F, by the construction. And the angles at E are vertically opposite, so they are equal. Two sides and the angle between them match, so the triangles are congruent. Every other matching pair of parts is now equal too.

slides.heading: Proof, step 3: a parallelogram appears
slides.body_md: Use the matching parts of the congruent triangles.

rows: D is the mid-point of AB
corresponding parts, so alternate angles: $AB \parallel CF$

visual.alt: Table with six claims and reasons that lead from the congruent triangles to the parallelogram B D F C and then to the conclusion D E parallel to B C and equal to half of it.

slides.narration: From the congruent triangles, C F equals A D. But A D equals D B, because D is the mid-point of A B. So C F equals D B. The angles at D and F are equal and alternate, so C F is parallel to A B. Now B D F C has a pair of opposite sides equal and parallel, so it is a parallelogram. Then D F is parallel and equal to B C, and D E is half of D F.

slides.heading: Quick check: state the theorem
slides.body_md: Which statement is the mid-point theorem?
slides.narration: Which statement is the mid-point theorem? Look for the one that says parallel to the third side and half as long. One option is the converse, which is a different statement, and one gets the length wrong.

slides.heading: Reading the theorem: three facts
slides.body_md: Because $DE \parallel BC$, corresponding angles are equal: $\angle ADE = \angle ABC$ (one arc) and $\angle AED = \angle ACB$ (two arcs).
bullets: $DE \parallel BC$
$DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$
Corresponding angles at $D$, $B$ and at $E$, $C$ are equal

visual.alt: Triangle A B C with D E joining the mid-points of A B and A C and parallel to B C. The angle A D E carries one arc and equals the angle A B C, which also carries one arc. The angle A E D carries two arcs and equals the angle A C B.
visual.caption: Corresponding angles: angle ADE = angle ABC and angle AED = angle ACB.

slides.narration: The theorem gives three facts. D E is parallel to B C. D E is half of B C. And, because the lines are parallel, corresponding angles are equal. The angle at D equals the angle at B, shown with one arc, and the angle at E equals the angle at C, shown with two arcs. Be careful to match angles at the correct vertices.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: finding a length
slides.body_md: In $\triangle PQR$, $S$ and $T$ are the mid-points of $PQ$ and $PR$, and $ST = 6.5$ cm. Find $QR$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $S$ and $T$ are mid-points, so $ST \parallel QR$ and $ST = \dfrac{1}{2}QR$.
**Step 2 —** $QR = 2 \times ST = 2 \times 6.5$.
**Answer —** $QR = 13$ cm.

visual.alt: Triangle P Q R with S and T the mid-points of P Q and P R. S T is parallel to Q R and measures six point five centimetres. Q R is to be found.
visual.caption: Drawn to scale: S T = 6.5 cm.

slides.narration: In triangle P Q R, S and T are the mid-points of P Q and P R, and S T is six point five centimetres. By the mid-point theorem, S T is half of Q R. So Q R is twice six point five, which is thirteen centimetres. Notice that we double, because the joining segment is the shorter one.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: an equation
slides.body_md: $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$. $DE = (2x + 1)$ cm and $BC = (5x - 7)$ cm. Find $x$ and the two lengths.

visual.alt: Table of five steps for finding x when D E equals two x plus one and B C equals five x minus seven: B C is twice D E, so x is nine, D E is nineteen and B C is thirty eight.

slides.narration: Here the lengths are given with x. By the mid-point theorem, B C is twice D E. So five x minus seven equals two times two x plus one. That simplifies to four x plus two. Solving gives x equals nine. Then D E is nineteen and B C is thirty eight. Check: twice nineteen is thirty eight.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding angles
slides.body_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle B = 54^\circ$ and $\angle C = 71^\circ$. $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$. Find $p = \angle ADE$ and $q = \angle DEC$.

visual.alt: Triangle A B C with angle B equal to fifty four degrees and angle C equal to seventy one degrees. D and E are the mid-points of A B and A C. The angle A D E is marked p and the angle D E C is marked q.
visual.caption: Find p = angle ADE and q = angle DEC.

slides.narration: Because D E is parallel to B C, the angle A D E equals the angle at B, which is fifty four degrees. The angle A E D equals the angle at C, seventy one degrees. The angle D E C lies on a straight line with A E D, so it is one hundred eighty minus seventy one, which is one hundred nine degrees. The angle at A is fifty five degrees.

slides.heading: The triangle of mid-points
slides.body_md: Join the mid-points $D$, $E$, $F$ of the three sides. Each side of $\triangle DEF$ is **parallel to a side of $\triangle ABC$ and half as long**.

visual.alt: Triangle A B C with D, E, F the mid-points of B C, C A and A B. The mid-point triangle D E F is shaded. Matching tick marks show that each side of D E F is half of a side of A B C and parallel to it.
visual.caption: Triangle D E F of mid-points: each of its sides is half a side of A B C.

slides.narration: Now join all three mid-points. This makes a smaller triangle D E F inside triangle A B C. Apply the theorem three times. D E is parallel to A B and half of it. E F is parallel to B C and half of it. F D is parallel to C A and half of it. The tick marks show the matching halves.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the perimeter is half
slides.body_md: A triangular sail has sides $6.8$ m, $9$ m and $11.6$ m. A ribbon joins the mid-points of its sides. Find the length of the ribbon.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Each piece is half the side parallel to it: $3.4$, $4.5$, $5.8$.

visual.alt: Table for a triangle with sides six point eight, nine and eleven point six. The joining lines parallel to them are three point four, four point five and five point eight, and the perimeters are twenty seven point four and thirteen point seven.

slides.narration: A sail has sides six point eight, nine and eleven point six metres. A ribbon runs along the three lines joining mid-points. Each piece is half of the side it is parallel to: three point four, four point five and five point eight. The total is thirteen point seven metres, which is exactly half of the perimeter of the sail, twenty seven point four.

slides.heading: Quick check: parallel is not equal
slides.body_md: Read the claim carefully and decide whether it is true.
slides.narration: Priya says that because D E is parallel to B C, D E must equal B C. Decide whether this is true or false. Remember what the theorem says about the length of the joining segment.

slides.heading: The quadrilateral of mid-points
slides.body_md: $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ are the mid-points of the sides of **any** quadrilateral $ABCD$. Then $PQRS$ is a **parallelogram**, with sides parallel to the diagonals.

visual.alt: Quadrilateral A B C D with its diagonals A C and B D dashed. P, Q, R, S are the mid-points of A B, B C, C D, D A. The shaded quadrilateral P Q R S has P Q and S R parallel to A C and equal, and Q R and P S parallel to B D and equal.
visual.caption: P Q R S is a parallelogram; its sides are parallel to the diagonals.

slides.narration: Now take any quadrilateral A B C D and join the mid-points of its four sides in order, giving P Q R S. The diagonals are dashed. Side P Q and side S R are both parallel to the diagonal A C and half as long. Side Q R and side P S are both parallel to the diagonal B D and half as long. So P Q R S is always a parallelogram.

slides.heading: Why P Q R S is a parallelogram
slides.body_md: Use the diagonal $AC$ in two triangles.

rows: both equal and parallel to the same thing
one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel
the same argument with the diagonal $BD$

visual.alt: Table of six steps showing that the mid-point quadrilateral P Q R S is a parallelogram, using the diagonal A C in two triangles and then the diagonal B D.

slides.narration: Join the diagonal A C. In triangle A B C, P and Q are mid-points, so P Q is parallel to A C and half of it. In triangle A D C, S and R are mid-points, so S R is parallel to A C and half of it. So P Q and S R are equal and parallel, and P Q R S is a parallelogram. The diagonal B D gives the other pair in the same way.

slides.heading: Special cases
slides.body_md: The sides of $PQRS$ are half the **diagonals** of $ABCD$ and parallel to them, so the shape of $ABCD$ decides the shape of $PQRS$.

visual.alt: Table of special cases: any diagonals give a parallelogram, equal diagonals a rhombus, perpendicular diagonals a rectangle, and equal and perpendicular diagonals a square.

slides.narration: The sides of the mid-point quadrilateral are half the diagonals and parallel to them. So the diagonals decide its shape. If the diagonals are equal, all four sides are equal and we get a rhombus. If the diagonals are perpendicular, adjacent sides are perpendicular and we get a rectangle. If the diagonals are both equal and perpendicular, we get a square.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a kite frame
slides.body_md: The diagonals of a kite $ABCD$ are perpendicular, with $AC = 16$ cm and $BD = 10$ cm. Its side mid-points form $PQRS$. Name it and find its perimeter and area.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Sides are $8$ cm and $5$ cm, parallel to the diagonals.
**Step 2 —** The diagonals are perpendicular, so $PQRS$ is a rectangle.
**Answer —** perimeter $2(8 + 5) = 26$ cm; area $8 \times 5 = 40$ cm$^{2}$.

visual.alt: A kite A B C D with perpendicular diagonals A C of sixteen centimetres and B D of ten centimetres, dashed. The mid-points P, Q, R, S of its sides are joined to form a shaded rectangle.
visual.caption: Drawn to scale: the shaded figure is a rectangle.

slides.narration: A kite has perpendicular diagonals of sixteen and ten centimetres. The mid-point quadrilateral has sides parallel to the diagonals and half as long, so eight and five centimetres. Since the diagonals are perpendicular, adjacent sides are perpendicular, so it is a rectangle. The perimeter is twenty six centimetres, and the area is eight times five, which is forty square centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: a ladder crossbar
slides.body_md: Apply the theorem to a real object.
slides.narration: An A shaped ladder has its feet one point three metres apart. A crossbar joins the mid-points of the two legs. Use the theorem to find how long the crossbar is, in metres.

slides.heading: Summary of part 1
slides.body_md: The mid-point theorem is the key: every result in this part is one or more uses of it.

rows: produce $DE$ to $F$ with $EF = DE$; congruent triangles; parallelogram $BDFC$
each side half of a side; perimeter half

visual.alt: Summary table of part one: the mid-point theorem, its proof, the triangle of mid-points, the quadrilateral of mid-points and the special cases.

slides.narration: Here is the summary of part one. The mid-point theorem says the joining segment is parallel to the third side and half as long. We proved it by doubling the segment and building a parallelogram. The triangle of mid-points has half the perimeter. The quadrilateral of mid-points is a parallelogram, with special cases for equal and perpendicular diagonals. Part two reverses the theorem.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Proof (about 4 to 6 marks):** construction 1, congruent triangles with the reason 1 or 2, parallelogram 1, conclusion 1
**Lengths (2 marks):** name the theorem 1 + double or halve 1
**Always** write the reason beside every statement
**Mistake:** $DE = BC$ instead of $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$
**Mistake:** halving when you should double, or the reverse

rows: perimeter of the mid-point triangle equals the perimeter
a parallelogram; a rectangle only for perpendicular diagonals

visual.alt: Table of four common slips in part one and their corrections: D E is half of B C, angle A D E equals angle A B C, the perimeter of the mid-point triangle is half, and the mid-point quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

slides.narration: Here is how marks are awarded. A proof is marked step by step: the construction, the congruent triangles with their reason, the parallelogram, and the conclusion. For a length question, name the theorem, then double or halve. Write a reason beside every statement. The two common mistakes are writing the joining segment equal to the third side, and halving when you should double.

decks.title: Mid-Point and Intercept Theorems — Part 2: The converse and the equal intercept theorem
goals: State and prove the converse of the mid-point theorem and apply it
Explain why the mid-point matters and why the parallel is needed
State and prove the equal intercept theorem
Divide a line segment into equal parts and use the mid-line results of a trapezium

slides.heading: Mid-point and intercept theorems, Part 2
slides.body_md: Now we go the other way: from **one mid-point and a parallel line** to the **second mid-point**.

visual.alt: Triangle A B C with D the mid-point of A B. The line through D parallel to B C meets A C at E, and equal tick marks show that E is the mid-point of A C.
visual.caption: The line through D parallel to B C bisects A C.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. In part one we started with two mid-points and found a parallel line. Now we go the other way. If a line passes through one mid-point and is parallel to a side, we shall see that it lands on a second mid-point. Then we meet the equal intercept theorem and use it to cut a segment into equal parts.

slides.heading: The converse
slides.body_md: The **converse** of a theorem swaps what is given with what is proved.

rows: If $D$ and $E$ are mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$
If $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $DE \parallel BC$ with $E$ on $AC$

visual.alt: Table that sets the mid-point theorem beside its converse. The theorem goes from two mid-points to parallel and half. The converse goes from one mid-point and a parallel to the second mid-point.

slides.narration: The converse of a theorem swaps what is given with what is proved. The mid-point theorem starts with two mid-points and ends with a parallel line, half as long. Its converse starts with one mid-point and a parallel line, and ends with the second mid-point. A converse is a new statement, so it needs its own proof.

slides.heading: The converse of the mid-point theorem
slides.body_md:
**Theorem.** A line drawn through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, **parallel** to a second side, **bisects** the third side.

In $\triangle ABC$, if $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $DE \parallel BC$ with $E$ on $AC$, then $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$.

visual.alt: Triangle A B C with D the mid-point of A B. The line through D parallel to B C meets A C at E, and equal tick marks show that E is the mid-point of A C.
visual.caption: The line through D parallel to B C bisects A C.

slides.narration: Here is the converse. In triangle A B C, D is the mid-point of A B. The line through D parallel to B C meets A C at E. Then E is the mid-point of A C. In the drawing the tick marks on A D and D B are given, and the tick marks on A E and E C are what we must prove. Both the mid-point and the parallel are needed.

slides.heading: Proof of the converse
slides.body_md: We show that the point $E$ is forced to be the mid-point.

rows: Let $E'$ be the mid-point of $AC$; join $DE'$
only one line through $D$ is parallel to $BC$
both are where that line meets $AC$

visual.alt: Table of six steps proving the converse of the mid-point theorem: take the mid-point E dash of A C, show D E dash is parallel to B C, note that only one such line passes through D, so E and E dash coincide.

slides.narration: Let E dash be the mid-point of A C and join D to E dash. By the mid-point theorem, D E dash is parallel to B C. But D E is also parallel to B C, by what is given. Through the point D there is only one line parallel to B C, so D E and D E dash are the same line. Both E and E dash are where that line meets A C, so they are the same point. Hence E is the mid-point.

slides.heading: Quick check: the converse
slides.body_md: Pick the statement that is the converse, not the theorem.
slides.narration: Which statement is the converse of the mid-point theorem? Remember the converse starts from one mid-point and a parallel line. Check that your choice keeps both words, mid-point and parallel.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: using the converse
slides.body_md: $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$, $DE \parallel BC$ and $E$ lies on $AC$. $DE = 5.9$ cm and $AC = 17.4$ cm. Find $AE$ and $BC$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $DE \parallel BC$ from the mid-point $D$, so $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$.
**Step 2 —** $AE = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 17.4 = 8.7$ cm.
**Answer —** $BC = 2 \times 5.9 = 11.8$ cm (mid-point theorem).

visual.alt: Triangle A B C with D the mid-point of A B. The line D E is parallel to B C, meets A C at E, and measures five point nine centimetres.
visual.caption: Drawn to scale: D E = 5.9 cm.

slides.narration: D is the mid-point of A B, and D E is parallel to B C, with E on A C. By the converse, E is the mid-point of A C, so A E is half of seventeen point four, which is eight point seven centimetres. Now D and E are mid-points, so the mid-point theorem gives B C as twice five point nine, which is eleven point eight centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: an equation
slides.body_md: In the same figure $AE = (2x + 5)$ cm and $EC = (4x - 7)$ cm. Find $x$ and $AC$.

visual.alt: Table of four steps: the converse gives A E equals E C, so two x plus five equals four x minus seven, x is six, each part is seventeen and A C is thirty four.

slides.narration: By the converse, E is the mid-point of A C, so A E equals E C. That gives two x plus five equals four x minus seven. Solving, x is six. Then A E and E C are each seventeen, and A C is thirty four centimetres. Always check: two times six plus five is seventeen, and four times six minus seven is seventeen.

slides.heading: Why the mid-point matters
slides.body_md: A line parallel to $BC$ cuts $AB$ and $AC$ in the **same ratio**. It reaches the mid-point of $AC$ only when it starts at the mid-point of $AB$.

visual.alt: Table showing that a line through D parallel to B C meets A C in the same ratio as D divides A B: one to one, one to two and one to three. Only the first case gives a mid-point.

slides.narration: Why must D be a mid-point? A line parallel to B C cuts A B and A C in the same ratio. If D is one third of the way along A B, the parallel meets A C one third of the way along, not half way. Only when D is the mid-point, a one to one ratio, does the parallel reach the mid-point of A C. The word parallel is needed too.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: two steps in a row
slides.body_md: $P$ is the mid-point of $XY$, $PQ \parallel YZ$ meets $XZ$ at $Q$, and $QR \parallel XY$ meets $YZ$ at $R$. $XY = 9.4$ cm and $YZ = 12.6$ cm. Find $PQ$, $QR$ and the perimeter of $PYRQ$.

visual.alt: Triangle X Y Z with P the mid-point of X Y. The line P Q is parallel to Y Z and meets X Z at Q, and the line Q R is parallel to X Y and meets Y Z at R. Tick marks show that Q is the mid-point of X Z and R is the mid-point of Y Z.
visual.caption: Two uses of the converse: Q and then R are mid-points.

slides.narration: Use the converse twice. P is the mid-point of X Y and P Q is parallel to Y Z, so Q is the mid-point of X Z. Then Q R is parallel to X Y, so R is the mid-point of Y Z. By the mid-point theorem P Q is half of twelve point six, which is six point three, and Q R is half of nine point four, which is four point seven. The parallelogram has perimeter twenty two.

slides.heading: The equal intercept theorem
slides.body_md: **Theorem.** If three or more parallel lines make **equal intercepts** on one transversal, they make equal intercepts on **every** transversal. A line crossing the parallel lines is a **transversal**; the part between two lines is an **intercept**.
bullets: Given: $l \parallel m \parallel n \parallel p$ and $AB = BC = CD$
To prove: $PQ = QR = RS$
The transversals need **not** be parallel to each other

visual.alt: Four parallel lines, marked with the same arrow, cut two transversals. On the left transversal the intercepts A B, B C and C D are equal. On the right transversal the intercepts P Q, Q R and R S are also equal, as the tick marks show.
visual.caption: Equal intercepts on one transversal give equal intercepts on every transversal.

slides.narration: Look at the four parallel lines. A line crossing them is a transversal, and the part between two lines is an intercept. On the left transversal the three intercepts are equal, and the tick marks show that the three intercepts on the right are equal too. That is the equal intercept theorem: equal intercepts on one transversal force equal intercepts on every other transversal. The two transversals do not have to be parallel to each other.

slides.heading: Proof, step 1: the construction
slides.body_md: Take three lines $l \parallel m \parallel n$ with $AB = BC$. Through $A$ draw a line **parallel to $PR$**, meeting $m$ at $S$ and $n$ at $T$.

visual.alt: Three parallel lines marked with arrows cut one transversal at A, B, C with A B equal to B C and a second transversal at P, Q, R. A dashed line through A, parallel to P R, meets the second and third lines at S and T. The parallelograms A P Q S and S Q R T are shaded.
visual.caption: Construction: through A draw a line parallel to P R.

slides.narration: Take three parallel lines with A B equal to B C. The second transversal meets them at P, Q and R. Through A we draw a dashed line parallel to P R. It meets the second line at S and the third line at T. The plan is to show that P Q equals A S, that Q R equals S T, and that S is the mid-point of A T.

slides.heading: Proof, step 2: two parallelograms
slides.body_md: The shaded figures are parallelograms.

visual.alt: Table of the two parallelograms in the proof of the equal intercept theorem: A P Q S gives A S equal to P Q, and S Q R T gives S T equal to Q R.

slides.narration: Look at the shaded figures. A P Q S has A P parallel to S Q, because the first two lines are parallel, and A S parallel to P Q by the construction. So it is a parallelogram, and A S equals P Q. In the same way S Q R T is a parallelogram, because the second and third lines are parallel and S T is parallel to Q R. So S T equals Q R.

slides.heading: Proof, step 3: the converse finishes it
slides.body_md: Now compare $AS$ and $ST$ inside $\triangle ACT$.

notes.title: Mid-Point and Intercept Theorems — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. The mid-point theorem
sections.body_md:
The segment joining the **mid-points of two sides** of a triangle is **parallel to the third side** and **half as long**.

In $\triangle ABC$, if $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$, then $DE \parallel BC$ and $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$.

- Because $DE \parallel BC$, corresponding angles are equal: $\angle ADE = \angle ABC$ and $\angle AED = \angle ACB$.
- The joining segment is always the **shorter** one: to find $BC$ from $DE$ you **double**.

key_terms.definition_md: The point that cuts a segment into two equal halves.
The segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half of it.

visual.alt: Triangle A B C with B C eight centimetres. D and E are the mid-points of A B and A C and D E measures four centimetres, half of B C, and is parallel to it.
visual.caption: Drawn to scale: B C is 8 cm and D E is 4 cm.

sections.heading: 2. Proof of the mid-point theorem
sections.body_md:
**Construction.** Produce $DE$ to $F$ so that $EF = DE$, and join $CF$.

1. $\triangle AED \cong \triangle CEF$: $AE = EC$, $DE = EF$ and $\angle AED = \angle CEF$ (vertically opposite): side angle side.
2. So $CF = AD = DB$ and $\angle ADE = \angle CFE$, which are alternate angles, so $CF \parallel AB$.
3. $BDFC$ has $BD$ and $CF$ equal and parallel: it is a **parallelogram**. So $DF \parallel BC$ and $DF = BC$.
4. $E$ is the mid-point of $DF$, so $DE \parallel BC$ and $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}DF = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$.

key_terms.definition_md: A helper point or line added to a figure so that a proof can use known results.

visual.alt: The proof figure. Triangle A B C has D and E the mid-points of A B and A C. D E is produced to F so that E F equals D E, and C F is joined. Triangles A E D and C E F are shaded and have equal tick marks on their matching sides.
visual.caption: Construction: produce D E to F so that E F = D E, then join C F.

sections.heading: 3. Triangle and quadrilateral of mid-points
sections.body_md:
**Triangle of mid-points.** If $D$, $E$, $F$ are the mid-points of $BC$, $CA$, $AB$, each side of $\triangle DEF$ is half of, and parallel to, a side of $\triangle ABC$. Its **perimeter is half** the perimeter of $\triangle ABC$ (for sides $6.8$, $9$, $11.6$ the triangle of mid-points has sides $3.4$, $4.5$, $5.8$, perimeter $13.7$).

**Quadrilateral of mid-points.** The mid-points $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ of the sides of **any** quadrilateral $ABCD$ form a **parallelogram**: $PQ$ and $SR$ are parallel to $AC$ and half of it, $QR$ and $PS$ are parallel to $BD$ and half of it.

- Equal diagonals: $PQRS$ is a **rhombus**. Perpendicular diagonals: a **rectangle**. Both: a **square**.

key_terms.definition_md: The triangle formed by joining the mid-points of the three sides of a triangle.
The quadrilateral formed by joining the mid-points of the sides of a quadrilateral in order; it is always a parallelogram.

visual.alt: Quadrilateral A B C D with its diagonals A C and B D dashed. P, Q, R, S are the mid-points of A B, B C, C D, D A. The shaded quadrilateral P Q R S has P Q and S R parallel to A C and equal, and Q R and P S parallel to B D and equal.
visual.caption: P Q R S is a parallelogram; its sides are parallel to the diagonals.

sections.heading: 4. The converse of the mid-point theorem
sections.body_md:
A line drawn through the **mid-point of one side** of a triangle, **parallel to a second side**, **bisects the third side**.

If $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $DE \parallel BC$ with $E$ on $AC$, then $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$ (and $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$).

**Proof.** Let $E'$ be the mid-point of $AC$. By the mid-point theorem $DE' \parallel BC$. Through $D$ there is only one line parallel to $BC$, so $DE$ and $DE'$ are the same line and $E = E'$.

- **Both conditions are needed.** A line parallel to $BC$ from a point one third of the way along $AB$ meets $AC$ one third of the way along; a slanted line through the mid-point $D$ misses the mid-point of $AC$.
- Chains: use the converse twice, for example $PQ \parallel YZ$ then $QR \parallel XY$ gives two mid-points.

key_terms.definition_md: A statement that swaps what is given and what is to be proved in a theorem.
To cut into two equal parts.

visual.alt: Triangle A B C with D the mid-point of A B. The line through D parallel to B C meets A C at E, and equal tick marks show that E is the mid-point of A C.
visual.caption: The line through D parallel to B C bisects A C.

sections.heading: 5. The equal intercept theorem
sections.body_md:
If **parallel lines** make **equal intercepts** on one transversal, they make equal intercepts on **every** transversal.

**Proof (three lines).** Let $AB = BC$ on one transversal, with $P$, $Q$, $R$ on another. Draw a line through $A$ parallel to $PR$, meeting the second and third lines at $S$ and $T$. Then $APQS$ and $SQRT$ are parallelograms, so $PQ = AS$ and $QR = ST$. In $\triangle ACT$, $B$ is the mid-point of $AC$ and $BS \parallel CT$, so by the converse $S$ is the mid-point of $AT$: $AS = ST$. Hence $PQ = QR$.

- With $n$ parallel lines there are $n - 1$ intercepts: divide by $n - 1$, not by $n$.
- The transversals need not be parallel to each other.

key_terms.definition_md: A line that crosses two or more other lines.
The part of a transversal between two of the parallel lines.

visual.alt: Three parallel lines marked with arrows cut one transversal at A, B, C with A B equal to B C and a second transversal at P, Q, R. A dashed line through A, parallel to P R, meets the second and third lines at S and T. The parallelograms A P Q S and S Q R T are shaded.
visual.caption: Construction: through A draw a line parallel to P R.

sections.heading: 6. Dividing a segment into equal parts
sections.body_md:
To divide $AB$ into $n$ equal parts:

1. Draw a ray from $A$ at an angle to $AB$.
2. Mark $n$ equal steps on the ray.
3. Join the last mark to $B$.
4. Through the other $n - 1$ marks draw lines parallel to this join; they cut $AB$ into $n$ equal parts, by the equal intercept theorem.

For $AB = 7.5$ cm and $n = 5$, each part is $1.5$ cm.

key_terms.definition_md: Parts of a segment that all have the same length.

visual.alt: Segment A B divided into five equal parts. From A a ray is marked with five equal steps numbered one to five. The last mark five is joined to B, and lines parallel to it through marks one to four cut A B at P, Q, R and S.
visual.caption: Lines parallel to M5 B through the marks 1, 2, 3, 4 cut A B into five equal parts.

sections.heading: 7. The trapezium results
sections.body_md:
In trapezium $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel DC$, the segment $MN$ joining the mid-points of the legs is **parallel to the bases** and equals **half their sum**.

- **Proof.** Produce $AN$ to meet $DC$ produced at $E$. $\triangle ABN \cong \triangle ECN$, so $CE = AB$ and $N$ is the mid-point of $AE$. In $\triangle ADE$, $MN = \dfrac{1}{2}DE = \dfrac{1}{2}(DC + AB)$.
- The line through the mid-point of one leg parallel to the bases bisects the other leg (equal intercept theorem).
- The mid-points of the **diagonals** lie on $MN$ and are $\dfrac{1}{2}(DC - AB)$ apart.

key_terms.definition_md: A quadrilateral with one pair of parallel sides (the bases); the other two sides are the legs.
The segment joining the mid-points of the legs of a trapezium.

visual.alt: Trapezium A B C D with A B parallel to D C. M and N are the mid-points of the legs. The diagonals A C and B D are dashed and their mid-points P and Q lie on M N.
visual.caption: The mid-points P and Q of the diagonals lie on M N.

sections.heading: 8. Exam tips and common mistakes
sections.body_md:
**Mark split.** A proof question is marked by step: the construction (1), each congruence or parallel statement with its reason (1 each), the conclusion (1). Always write the **reason** next to every statement.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing $DE = BC$ instead of $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$.
- Using the converse without both conditions: the line must start at the **mid-point** and be **parallel**.
- Matching the wrong angles: $\angle ADE = \angle ABC$, not $\angle ACB$.
- Dividing by $n$ instead of $n - 1$ when counting intercepts between $n$ parallel lines.
- Forgetting that the mid-point quadrilateral is a **parallelogram** only, and a rectangle or rhombus only for special diagonals.
- Giving the perimeter of the mid-point triangle as the perimeter of the original, or doubling instead of halving.
- Using coordinates in a proof: here the proofs use congruent triangles and parallel lines.

key_terms.definition_md: The earlier result that justifies a step of a proof.

visual.caption: The mid-point theorem

cards.front_md: What is the **mid-point theorem**?
cards.back_md: The segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half of it: $DE \parallel BC$, $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$.

cards.front_md: What is the **converse** of the mid-point theorem?
cards.back_md: A line through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel to a second side, bisects the third side.

cards.front_md: What is an **intercept**?
cards.back_md: The part of a transversal between two of the parallel lines that it crosses.

cards.front_md: What is a **transversal**?
cards.back_md: A line that crosses two or more other lines.

cards.front_md: What is the **mid-line** of a trapezium?
cards.back_md: The segment joining the mid-points of its two non-parallel sides (the legs).

cards.front_md: What is the **equal intercept theorem**?
cards.back_md: If parallel lines make equal intercepts on one transversal, they make equal intercepts on every transversal.

cards.front_md: Formula for the mid-point theorem?
cards.back_md: $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$ and $DE \parallel BC$.

cards.front_md: Perimeter of the triangle of mid-points?
cards.back_md: Half the perimeter of the original triangle.

cards.front_md: Sides of the quadrilateral of mid-points $PQRS$?
cards.back_md: $PQ = SR = \dfrac{1}{2}AC$ and $QR = PS = \dfrac{1}{2}BD$, parallel to the diagonals.

cards.front_md: Mid-line of a trapezium with parallel sides $a$ and $b$?
Segment joining the mid-points of the diagonals of a trapezium?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{1}{2}(b - a)$, half of the difference of the parallel sides ($b > a$).

cards.front_md: Length of each part when $AB$ is divided into $n$ equal parts?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{AB}{n}$.

cards.front_md: Why is $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$ in the proof?
cards.back_md: $E$ is the mid-point of $DF$ and $DF = BC$ (parallelogram $BDFC$), so $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}DF = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$.

cards.front_md: What construction proves the mid-point theorem?
cards.back_md: Produce $DE$ to $F$ so that $EF = DE$ and join $CF$.

cards.front_md: Which triangles are congruent in that proof, and by what condition?
cards.back_md: $\triangle AED \cong \triangle CEF$ by side angle side: $AE = EC$, $DE = EF$, vertically opposite angles at $E$.

cards.front_md: Why is the mid-point needed in the converse?
cards.back_md: A line parallel to $BC$ cuts $AB$ and $AC$ in the same ratio; it reaches the mid-point of $AC$ only when it starts at the mid-point of $AB$.

cards.front_md: Why is the word parallel needed in the converse?
cards.back_md: A slanted line through the mid-point $D$ meets $AC$ at some other point; only the parallel meets it at the mid-point.

cards.front_md: How does the proof of the converse work?
cards.back_md: Take the mid-point $E'$ of $AC$; $DE' \parallel BC$ by the theorem; only one line through $D$ is parallel to $BC$, so $E = E'$.

cards.front_md: Does the equal intercept theorem need parallel transversals?
cards.back_md: No. The transversals can be any two lines that cross the parallel lines.

cards.front_md: What does the proof of the equal intercept theorem use?
cards.back_md: Two parallelograms (to move the intercepts onto one line) and the converse of the mid-point theorem.

cards.front_md: Triangle of mid-points of an equilateral triangle of side $14$ cm?
cards.back_md: An equilateral triangle of side $7$ cm: perimeter $21$ cm.

cards.front_md: The mid-points of the sides of a rectangle (not a square) are joined. What is formed?
cards.back_md: A rhombus (the diagonals are equal), not a square.

cards.front_md: The diagonals of a quadrilateral are perpendicular. What is $PQRS$?
cards.back_md: A rectangle (adjacent sides are parallel to perpendicular diagonals).

cards.front_md: How many intercepts do five parallel lines make?
cards.back_md: Four. Divide the total by $4$, not by $5$.

cards.front_md: Worked: $DE = 5.9$ cm in the converse figure. Find $BC$.
cards.back_md: $BC = 2 \times 5.9 = 11.8$ cm (double the joining segment).

cards.front_md: Worked: $AE = (2x + 5)$ and $EC = (4x - 7)$ with $E$ the mid-point of $AC$.
Worked: parallel sides $9.6$ and $17.2$. Find the mid-line.
Common slip when using the angles in the mid-point figure?
cards.back_md: Writing $\angle ADE = \angle ACB$. The correct pair is $\angle ADE = \angle ABC$ (corresponding angles at $D$ and $B$).

cards.front_md: Common slip with the joining segment?
cards.back_md: Writing $DE = BC$. It is **half** of $BC$; to get $BC$ from $DE$ you double.

cards.front_md: Picture: what do the tick marks and arrows mean in the figures?
cards.back_md: Equal tick marks mean equal lengths (the mid-point halves); equal arrow marks mean parallel lines.

questions.stem_md: Which statement is the mid-point theorem?

options.text_md: The segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half as long as it.
The segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and equal to it.
The segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is perpendicular to the third side and half as long as it.
A line through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel to a second side, bisects the third side.

questions.solution_md: Join the mid-points $D$ and $E$ of two sides $AB$ and $AC$ of $\triangle ABC$. Then $DE \parallel BC$ and $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$. The wrong answers give the wrong length (equal to the third side), the wrong direction (perpendicular), or state the converse of the theorem, which is a different statement.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle XYZ$, $P$ and $Q$ are the mid-points of $XY$ and $XZ$ and $YZ = 15.6$ cm. The length of $PQ$ is
questions.solution_md: By the mid-point theorem $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}YZ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 15.6 = 7.8$ cm. The other values double, repeat or halve again.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$, and $\angle ACB = 68^\circ$. The angle $\angle DEC$ is
questions.solution_md: $DE \parallel BC$ by the mid-point theorem, with $AC$ as a transversal. The angles $\angle DEC$ and $\angle ECB$ are co-interior angles, so $\angle DEC = 180^\circ - 68^\circ = 112^\circ$. (The angle $68^\circ$ itself is $\angle AED$, a corresponding angle.)

assets.alt: Triangle A B C with D and E the mid-points of A B and A C. The angle at C measures sixty eight degrees and the angle D E C is marked x.
assets.caption: Angle A C B is 68 degrees; find angle D E C.

questions.stem_md: Anita ties a string between the mid-points of the two slanting sides of a triangular banner. The base of the banner is 1.84 m. The string is

options.text_md: 1.84 m long and parallel to the base
3.68 m long and parallel to the base
0.46 m long and parallel to the base
0.92 m long and parallel to the base

questions.solution_md: The string joins the mid-points of two sides of the triangle, so it is parallel to the base and half as long: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 1.84 = 0.92$ m.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, the point $D$ lies on $AB$ and the point $E$ lies on $AC$. In which situation is $E$ certain to be the mid-point of $AC$?

options.text_md: $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $DE \parallel BC$.
$D$ is any point of $AB$ and $DE \parallel BC$.
$D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $DE$ is any line through $D$.
$D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $DE \perp AB$.

questions.solution_md: This is the converse of the mid-point theorem: the line through the mid-point of one side, parallel to a second side, meets the third side at its mid-point. In the other three situations $E$ can lie elsewhere: if $D$ is one third of the way along $AB$, the parallel to $BC$ meets $AC$ one third of the way along; a line through the mid-point $D$ can meet $AC$ at other points; and a perpendicular to $AB$ at $D$ generally misses the mid-point of $AC$.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and the line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ meets $AC$ at $E$. If $AE = (3x + 1)$ cm and $EC = (5x - 9)$ cm, then $AC$ is
questions.solution_md: By the converse of the mid-point theorem $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$, so $AE = EC$: $3x + 1 = 5x - 9$, giving $x = 5$. Then $AE = 16$ cm, $EC = 16$ cm and $AC = 32$ cm. The value $16$ cm is only one half.

questions.stem_md: A triangular plate has sides 7.4 cm, 9.8 cm and 12.2 cm. Its three mid-points are joined to form a smaller triangle. The perimeter of the smaller triangle is
questions.solution_md: Each side of the triangle of mid-points is half of the side of the plate that is parallel to it. So its perimeter is half of $7.4 + 9.8 + 12.2 = 29.4$, which is $14.7$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The mid-points of the sides of an equilateral triangle of side 14 cm are joined to form a smaller triangle. Its perimeter is
questions.solution_md: Each side of the smaller triangle is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 14 = 7$ cm, so its perimeter is $3 \times 7 = 21$ cm (half of $42$ cm).

questions.stem_md: The mid-points of the four sides of a 9 cm by 4 cm rectangle are joined in order. The figure formed is

options.text_md: a rhombus that is not a square
a rectangle that is not a square
a parallelogram whose adjacent sides are unequal

questions.solution_md: The sides of the figure of mid-points are parallel to the diagonals of the rectangle and half as long. The diagonals of a rectangle are equal, so all four sides are equal: it is a rhombus. The diagonals of a $9$ by $4$ rectangle are not perpendicular, so the rhombus has no right angle and is not a square.

questions.stem_md: A kite-maker joins the mid-points of the four sides of a flat frame whose diagonals measure 9.2 cm and 6.4 cm. The perimeter of the figure formed by the joins is
questions.solution_md: The figure is a parallelogram with sides parallel to the diagonals and half as long: two sides of $4.6$ cm and two of $3.2$ cm. Its perimeter is $2(4.6 + 3.2) = 15.6$ cm, which is the sum of the two diagonals.

questions.stem_md: Three parallel lines cut off equal intercepts $AB = BC$ on one transversal. A second transversal meets the lines at $P$, $Q$ and $R$. Then
questions.solution_md: By the equal intercept theorem, parallel lines that cut equal intercepts on one transversal cut equal intercepts on every transversal, so $PQ = QR$. The intercepts $PQ$ and $QR$ need not equal $AB$ and lie along one straight line, so they are not parallel.

questions.stem_md: The three parallel rails of a gate are equally spaced along a slanting bar. A second bar crosses the rails at $P$, $Q$ and $R$ with $PR = 9.6$ cm. The length $PQ$ is
questions.solution_md: The rails are equally spaced along the first bar, so they make equal intercepts on the second bar: $PQ = QR$. Hence $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 9.6 = 4.8$ cm.

questions.stem_md: Five parallel lines make equal intercepts on one transversal. On a second transversal the first and the fifth line are 18.4 cm apart. The distance on this transversal between the second line and the fourth line is
questions.solution_md: The four intercepts on the second transversal are equal, each $\dfrac{18.4}{4} = 4.6$ cm. The second and fourth lines are two intercepts apart: $2 \times 4.6 = 9.2$ cm.

questions.stem_md: In trapezium $ABCD$, $AB \parallel DC$, $AB = 7.2$ cm and $DC = 11.6$ cm. $M$ and $N$ are the mid-points of the legs $AD$ and $BC$. The length $MN$ is
questions.solution_md: The segment joining the mid-points of the legs of a trapezium is parallel to the bases and equal to half of their sum: $MN = \dfrac{1}{2}(7.2 + 11.6) = 9.4$ cm. The value $18.8$ is the sum, $4.4$ is the difference.

questions.stem_md: The parallel sides of a trapezium are $(2x + 3)$ cm and $(4x - 1)$ cm long, and the line joining the mid-points of its legs is $13$ cm long. The shorter parallel side is
questions.solution_md: The mid-line is half the sum of the parallel sides: $\dfrac{(2x + 3) + (4x - 1)}{2} = 13$, so $6x + 2 = 26$ and $x = 4$. The parallel sides are $2(4) + 3 = 11$ cm and $4(4) - 1 = 15$ cm; the shorter is $11$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The parallel sides of a trapezium are 14 cm and 9 cm. The segment that joins the mid-points of its two diagonals is
questions.solution_md: The mid-points of the diagonals lie on the line joining the mid-points of the legs. Applying the mid-point theorem in the triangles formed by a diagonal shows that this segment is half of the difference of the parallel sides: $\dfrac{1}{2}(14 - 9) = 2.5$ cm. The value $11.5$ cm is the mid-line, which joins the mid-points of the legs.

questions.stem_md: Which statement is the converse of the mid-point theorem?

options.text_md: A line drawn through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel to a second side, bisects the third side.
The line joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side.
A line through the mid-point of one side of a triangle bisects the third side.
A line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle bisects the other two sides.

questions.solution_md: The converse says that if $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $DE \parallel BC$ with $E$ on $AC$, then $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$. Without the word parallel, or without the mid-point, the claim fails: a line through $D$ can meet $AC$ anywhere, and a line parallel to $BC$ cuts $AB$ and $AC$ in the same ratio, which need not be $1 : 1$.

questions.stem_md: Ravi says: "$D$ is a point on $AB$ and $E$ a point on $AC$ with $DE \parallel BC$, so $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$." What must be added for his statement to be correct?

options.text_md: $\angle ADE$ must be a right angle.

questions.solution_md: A line parallel to $BC$ cuts $AB$ and $AC$ in the same ratio, so $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$ exactly when $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$. Making the triangle isosceles, or $\angle ADE$ a right angle, does not help: with $D$ one third of the way along $AB$ the parallel still meets $AC$ one third of the way along. And $DE$ is always shorter than $BC$ here, whatever the position of $D$.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 10.4$ cm, $BC = 9.4$ cm and $CA = 7.2$ cm. $D$, $E$, $F$ are the mid-points of $BC$, $CA$, $AB$. The perimeter of the quadrilateral $AFDE$ is
questions.solution_md: $AFDE$ is a parallelogram, because $FD \parallel AC$ and $DE \parallel AB$ (mid-point theorem), with $AF = DE = \dfrac{1}{2}AB = 5.2$ cm and $AE = FD = \dfrac{1}{2}AC = 3.6$ cm. Its perimeter is $2(5.2 + 3.6) = 17.6$ cm, which equals $AB + AC$. The value $27$ cm would be the perimeter of $\triangle ABC$.

questions.stem_md: A segment AB is to be divided into 7 equal parts by drawing a ray from A, marking equal steps along it, joining the last mark to B and drawing parallels through the other marks. How many equal steps are marked on the ray?
questions.solution_md: To make $7$ equal parts we need $7$ equal steps on the ray. The last (seventh) mark is joined to $B$, and the six lines parallel to this join pass through marks $1$ to $6$ and cut $AB$ into $7$ equal parts.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle PQR$, $S$ is the mid-point of $PQ$. The line through $S$ parallel to $QR$ meets $PR$ at $T$, and the line through $T$ parallel to $PQ$ meets $QR$ at $U$. If $QR = 13.6$ cm, then $QU$ is
questions.solution_md: By the converse of the mid-point theorem in $\triangle PQR$, $T$ is the mid-point of $PR$. Now apply it again with $T$ and the line $TU \parallel PQ$: $U$ is the mid-point of $QR$. So $QU = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 13.6 = 6.8$ cm.

questions.stem_md: $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$ in a scalene $\triangle ABC$. Which of these statements is **not** true?
questions.solution_md: $DE \parallel BC$ and $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$ are the mid-point theorem. Since $DE \parallel BC$, $AB$ is a transversal and the corresponding angles are equal: $\angle ADE = \angle ABC$. The angle equal to $\angle ACB$ is $\angle AED$, so $\angle ADE = \angle ACB$ is false unless $AB = AC$, which a scalene triangle rules out.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In $\triangle ABC$, if $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$ and $DE = 5$ cm, then $BC = 10$ cm.

**Reason (R):** The segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is half of the third side.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: By the mid-point theorem $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$, so $BC = 2 \times 5 = 10$ cm. So A is true, R is true, and R is exactly the reason for A. Option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $E$ is a point of $AC$ with $DE \parallel BC$. Then $AE = EC$.

**Reason (R):** If a line through $D$ meets $AC$ at $E$, then $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: it is the converse of the mid-point theorem. R is false: a line through $D$ that is not parallel to $BC$ also meets $AC$, but then $DE$ is not parallel to $BC$ and has no reason to be half of it. Option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In $\triangle ABC$, if $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $E$ is a point of $AC$ with $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$, then $E$ must be the mid-point of $AC$.

**Reason (R):** The line through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel to a second side, meets the third side at its mid-point.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is true: it is the converse of the mid-point theorem. A is false: a circle of radius $\dfrac{1}{2}BC$ about $D$ cuts the line $AC$ in two points, and only one of them is the mid-point, so the length alone does not decide $E$. (R is also not a reason for A, because A does not mention parallel lines.) Option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In trapezium $ABCD$ with $AB \parallel DC$, the line joining the mid-points of the legs $AD$ and $BC$ is parallel to $AB$.

**Reason (R):** The line joining the mid-points of the legs of a trapezium is half of the sum of the parallel sides.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true and R is true. But R is a statement about length, while A is about direction, so R does not explain A. The parallelism is explained by the mid-point theorem applied in the triangle formed by joining $A$ to the mid-point of $BC$ and extending that line to meet $DC$ produced. Option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The mid-points of the sides of a quadrilateral whose diagonals are 10 cm and 6 cm form a parallelogram of perimeter 16 cm.

**Reason (R):** Each side of the parallelogram of mid-points is parallel to a diagonal of the quadrilateral and half as long.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: By R the sides of the parallelogram are $5$ cm, $3$ cm, $5$ cm and $3$ cm, so its perimeter is $16$ cm. A is true, and R is the reason. Option (c).

questions.stem_md: Priya joins the mid-points $D$ and $E$ of $AB$ and $AC$ in $\triangle ABC$ and says: "$DE \parallel BC$, so $DE = BC$."
questions.solution_md: Being parallel does not make the segments equal. By the mid-point theorem $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$, so $DE$ is only half as long.

questions.stem_md: The line joining the mid-points of the non-parallel sides of a trapezium is parallel to the parallel sides.
questions.solution_md: True: if $AB \parallel DC$ and $M$, $N$ are the mid-points of $AD$ and $BC$, then $MN \parallel AB \parallel DC$, and $MN = \dfrac{1}{2}(AB + DC)$.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, a line through the mid-point $D$ of $AB$ meets $AC$ at $E$. Then $E$ is always the mid-point of $AC$.
questions.solution_md: False. $E$ is the mid-point only when the line through $D$ is parallel to $BC$. A slanted line through $D$ meets $AC$ at some other point, so the word "parallel" cannot be dropped from the converse.

questions.stem_md: In the equal intercept theorem, the two transversals that cut the parallel lines need not be parallel to each other.
questions.solution_md: True. Any two lines that cross the parallel lines can serve as transversals; the theorem says that equal intercepts on one transversal force equal intercepts on the other. The transversals may even meet outside the figure.

questions.stem_md: If the diagonals of a quadrilateral are perpendicular, the quadrilateral formed by joining the mid-points of its sides is a rhombus.
questions.solution_md: False. The sides of the figure of mid-points are parallel to the diagonals, so perpendicular diagonals make adjacent sides perpendicular: the figure is a rectangle. It is a rhombus only if the diagonals are also equal; for diagonals of $10$ cm and $6$ cm its sides are $5$ cm and $3$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The two sloping legs of an A-shaped step-ladder have their feet $1.3$ m apart. A crossbar is fixed between the mid-points of the legs. The crossbar is ______ m long.
questions.solution_md: The crossbar joins the mid-points of two sides of the triangle formed by the legs and the floor, so it is half the third side: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 1.3 = 0.65$ m.

questions.stem_md: The mid-points of the sides of a quadrilateral whose diagonals are 11 cm and 7 cm are joined in order. The perimeter of the parallelogram formed is ______ cm.
questions.solution_md: Its sides are half the diagonals: $5.5$ cm and $3.5$ cm, each twice. The perimeter is $2(5.5 + 3.5) = 18$ cm.

questions.stem_md: In a trapezium the parallel sides are 8.5 cm and 13.7 cm. The line joining the mid-points of the other two sides is ______ cm long.
questions.solution_md: The mid-line is half the sum of the parallel sides: $\dfrac{1}{2}(8.5 + 13.7) = \dfrac{22.2}{2} = 11.1$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A segment AB is divided into 6 equal parts by the parallel-line method. Besides the line through the last mark of the ray (which passes through B), ______ parallel lines are drawn through the other marks.
questions.solution_md: There are $6$ marks on the ray. The sixth is joined to $B$; the lines through marks $1$ to $5$ are parallel to that join and cut $AB$ into $6$ equal parts. So $5$ more parallel lines are drawn.

questions.stem_md: The perimeter of a triangle is 38.6 cm. The triangle formed by joining the mid-points of its sides has perimeter ______ cm.
questions.solution_md: Each side of the triangle of mid-points is half of the parallel side of the original, so its perimeter is half: $\dfrac{38.6}{2} = 19.3$ cm.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 12.8$ cm, $BC = 18.4$ cm and $CA = 15.2$ cm. $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$. Find the perimeter of $\triangle ADE$, in cm.
questions.solution_md: $AD = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12.8 = 6.4$, $AE = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 15.2 = 7.6$ and $DE = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18.4 = 9.2$ (mid-point theorem). The perimeter is $6.4 + 7.6 + 9.2 = 23.2$ cm, half of the perimeter $46.4$ cm of $\triangle ABC$.

questions.stem_md: The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of a kite-shaped frame $ABCD$ are perpendicular, with $AC = 24$ cm and $BD = 18$ cm. The mid-points of its four sides are joined in order. Find the area, in cm$^{2}$, of the figure formed.
questions.solution_md: The figure of mid-points has sides parallel to the diagonals and half as long. As the diagonals are perpendicular, adjacent sides are perpendicular, so it is a rectangle $12$ cm by $9$ cm. Its area is $12 \times 9 = 108$ cm$^{2}$.

questions.stem_md: The line joining the mid-points of the legs of a trapezium is $14.5$ cm long, and one of the parallel sides is $10.2$ cm. Find the other parallel side, in cm.
questions.solution_md: The mid-line is half the sum of the parallel sides, so the sum is $2 \times 14.5 = 29$ cm. The other side is $29 - 10.2 = 18.8$ cm.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$. $DE = (3x - 2)$ cm and $BC = (5x + 6)$ cm. Find the length of $BC$, in cm.

Four parallel lines make equal intercepts on one transversal. On a second transversal the first and the fourth line are $16.5$ cm apart. Find the distance, in cm, between the first and the second line along the second transversal.
questions.solution_md: The three intercepts on the second transversal are equal (equal intercept theorem), so each is $\dfrac{16.5}{3} = 5.5$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The parallel sides of a trapezium are $19$ cm and $12.4$ cm. Find the length, in cm, of the segment that joins the mid-points of its diagonals.
questions.solution_md: The segment joining the mid-points of the diagonals lies along the mid-line of the trapezium and equals half of the difference of the parallel sides: $\dfrac{1}{2}(19 - 12.4) = \dfrac{6.6}{2} = 3.3$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: Half of the difference of the parallel sides

questions.stem_md: The area of $\triangle ABC$ is $76$ cm$^{2}$. Its three mid-points are joined to form a smaller triangle. Find the area of the smaller triangle, in cm$^{2}$.
questions.solution_md: The three lines joining the mid-points cut $\triangle ABC$ into four triangles that are congruent to the triangle of mid-points (each has sides half of $\triangle ABC$'s sides). The smaller triangle is one of four equal parts: $\dfrac{76}{4} = 19$ cm$^{2}$.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle XYZ$, $P$ and $Q$ are the mid-points of $XY$ and $XZ$. State the mid-point theorem for this triangle, giving both of its conclusions about $PQ$.

answer.model_answer_md: $PQ \parallel YZ$, and $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}YZ$: the segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half as long.

questions.solution_md: The mid-point theorem gives two facts about the segment $PQ$: its direction (parallel to the third side $YZ$) and its length (half of $YZ$).

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle KLM$, $P$ and $Q$ are the mid-points of $KL$ and $KM$. $PQ = 8.4$ cm and $\angle KLM = 64^\circ$. Find $LM$ and $\angle LPQ$, giving a reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
By the mid-point theorem $PQ \parallel LM$ and $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}LM$, so $LM = 2 \times 8.4 = 16.8$ cm.

Since $PQ \parallel LM$ and $KL$ is a transversal, $\angle LPQ$ and $\angle KLM$ are co-interior angles, so $\angle LPQ = 180^\circ - 64^\circ = 116^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: The mid-point theorem gives $LM$ from $PQ$ and the parallel lines give the angle: $\angle LPQ + \angle PLM = 180^\circ$ (co-interior angles).

marking_scheme.step: PQ parallel to LM; LM = 2 x 8.4 = 16.8 cm

questions.stem_md: State the converse of the mid-point theorem. In $\triangle PQR$, $S$ is the mid-point of $PQ$ and the line $ST \parallel QR$ meets $PR$ at $T$. If $PR = 18.6$ cm and $QR = 13.8$ cm, find $PT$ and $ST$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Converse: the line drawn through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel to a second side, bisects the third side.

So $T$ is the mid-point of $PR$: $PT = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18.6 = 9.3$ cm, and $ST = \dfrac{1}{2}QR = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 13.8 = 6.9$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Apply the converse to find $PT$ and then the mid-point theorem to find $ST$.

marking_scheme.step: Converse stated: a line through the mid-point of one side, parallel to another side, bisects the third side

questions.stem_md: Four parallel rails make equal intercepts on a slanting bar. A second bar crosses the rails at $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$, and $AB = 3.7$ cm. Find $AD$ and name the theorem you use.

answer.model_answer_md: By the equal intercept theorem the intercepts $AB$, $BC$ and $CD$ on the second bar are equal, each $3.7$ cm. So $AD = 3 \times 3.7 = 11.1$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Equal intercepts on one transversal give equal intercepts on every transversal, so the second bar is cut into three equal parts of $3.7$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: Equal intercept theorem: AB = BC = CD

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = AC = 10.6$ cm and $BC = 8.4$ cm. $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$. Name the quadrilateral $BDEC$ and find its perimeter.

answer.model_answer_md: $DE \parallel BC$ (mid-point theorem), so $BDEC$ is a trapezium; as $BD = EC = 5.3$ cm it is an isosceles trapezium. $DE = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 8.4 = 4.2$ cm, so the perimeter is $5.3 + 4.2 + 5.3 + 8.4 = 23.2$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The sides are $BD = \dfrac{1}{2}AB$, $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$, $EC = \dfrac{1}{2}AC$ and $CB$.

marking_scheme.step: DE parallel to BC, so a (isosceles) trapezium

questions.stem_md: Asha writes: "In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$, so $DE \parallel BC$ and $DE = BC$. Hence $BDEC$ is a parallelogram." Find her error and say what $BDEC$ really is when $BC = 10$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md: The mid-point theorem gives $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}BC$, not $DE = BC$. With $BC = 10$ cm, $DE = 5$ cm. So $BDEC$ has one pair of parallel sides, $DE$ and $BC$, which are unequal: it is a trapezium, not a parallelogram.

questions.solution_md: A parallelogram needs a pair of opposite sides that are both parallel and equal. Here $DE \parallel BC$ but $DE$ is half of $BC$.

marking_scheme.step: Error: DE = half of BC (DE = 5 cm), not BC
BDEC is a trapezium, not a parallelogram

questions.stem_md: In trapezium $ABCD$, $AB \parallel DC$. $P$ and $Q$ are the mid-points of the legs $AD$ and $BC$, $PQ = 10$ cm and $AB = 7$ cm. Find $DC$.

answer.model_answer_md: The segment joining the mid-points of the legs is half of the sum of the parallel sides: $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}(AB + DC)$. So $10 = \dfrac{1}{2}(7 + DC)$, $7 + DC = 20$ and $DC = 13$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Use $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}(AB + DC)$ and solve for $DC$.

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$, $E$, $F$ are the mid-points of $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ and $AB = 9.2$ cm. Find $AF$ and $DE$, and say why they are equal.

answer.model_answer_md: $F$ is the mid-point of $AB$, so $AF = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 9.2 = 4.6$ cm. $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $BC$ and $CA$, so by the mid-point theorem $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}AB = 4.6$ cm. Both equal half of $AB$, so $AF = DE$.

questions.solution_md: $AF$ is half of $AB$ by definition of mid-point, and $DE$ is half of $AB$ by the mid-point theorem in $\triangle ABC$.

marking_scheme.step: AF = 4.6 cm (F is the mid-point of AB)
DE = half of AB = 4.6 cm (mid-point theorem), so AF = DE

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$, $E$, $F$ are the mid-points of $BC$, $CA$, $AB$. Prove that $AFDE$ is a parallelogram.

answer.model_answer_md:
In $\triangle ABC$, $F$ and $D$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $BC$, so $FD \parallel AC$, that is $FD \parallel AE$.

Also $E$ and $D$ are the mid-points of $CA$ and $BC$, so $ED \parallel AB$, that is $ED \parallel AF$.

Both pairs of opposite sides of $AFDE$ are parallel, so $AFDE$ is a parallelogram.

questions.solution_md: Use the mid-point theorem twice, once for each pair of opposite sides.

marking_scheme.step: FD parallel to AC (mid-point theorem for F and D)
ED parallel to AB (mid-point theorem for E and D)
Both pairs of opposite sides parallel: parallelogram

questions.stem_md: A triangular sail has sides $5.6$ m, $7.2$ m and $8.8$ m. A sailor stitches a ribbon along the three lines that join the mid-points of its sides. Find the length of each piece of ribbon and the total length of ribbon used.

answer.model_answer_md: Each line joining mid-points is parallel to a side of the sail and half as long (mid-point theorem). The pieces are $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 5.6 = 2.8$ m, $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 7.2 = 3.6$ m and $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 8.8 = 4.4$ m. The total is $2.8 + 3.6 + 4.4 = 10.8$ m, which is half of the perimeter $21.6$ m of the sail.

questions.solution_md: Apply the mid-point theorem to each pair of sides.

marking_scheme.step: Each piece is half of the side parallel to it (mid-point theorem)

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and the line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ meets $AC$ at $E$. $AE = (2x + 3.5)$ cm, $EC = (5x - 6.7)$ cm and $DE = (3x - 1.5)$ cm. Find $x$, $AC$ and $BC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
By the converse of the mid-point theorem $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$, so $AE = EC$: $2x + 3.5 = 5x - 6.7$, giving $3x = 10.2$ and $x = 3.4$.

Then $AE = 10.3$ cm and $AC = 2 \times 10.3 = 20.6$ cm.

By the mid-point theorem $BC = 2\,DE = 2(3 \times 3.4 - 1.5) = 2 \times 8.7 = 17.4$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The converse gives $AE = EC$ (an equation for $x$), and the mid-point theorem gives $BC = 2\,DE$.

questions.stem_md: Describe, using parallel lines, how to divide a line segment $AB$ of length $7.5$ cm into three equal parts, and state the length of each part.

answer.model_answer_md:
Draw a ray from $A$ at an acute angle to $AB$. Mark off three equal steps along it with compasses, and number the marks $1$, $2$, $3$. Join the third mark $3$ to $B$, and through the marks $1$ and $2$ draw lines parallel to $3B$, meeting $AB$ at $P$ and $Q$.

These parallel lines cut the ray in equal intercepts (the three equal steps), so by the equal intercept theorem they make equal intercepts on $AB$: $AP = PQ = QB = 7.5 \div 3 = 2.5$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The construction is justified by the equal intercept theorem.

marking_scheme.step: Ray from A at an angle; three equal steps marked on it
3 joined to B; parallels through 1 and 2 meet AB at P and Q
Equal intercept theorem: AP = PQ = QB = 2.5 cm

questions.stem_md: In trapezium $ABCD$, $AB \parallel DC$ and $M$ is the mid-point of the leg $AD$. The line through $M$ parallel to $AB$ meets $BC$ at $N$. Prove that $N$ is the mid-point of $BC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The lines $AB$, $MN$ and $DC$ are parallel (as $MN \parallel AB \parallel DC$) and cut the transversal $AD$ in equal intercepts $AM = MD$.

By the equal intercept theorem they cut equal intercepts on the transversal $BC$ as well, so $BN = NC$.

Hence $N$ is the mid-point of $BC$.

questions.solution_md: Three parallel lines, equal intercepts on $AD$, therefore equal intercepts on $BC$.

marking_scheme.step: AB, MN, DC are parallel and AM = MD on transversal AD
Equal intercept theorem for the transversal BC
BN = NC, so N is the mid-point of BC

questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $M$ is the mid-point of $BC$, and $D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$. The segment $DE$ meets $AM$ at $P$. Prove that $P$ is the mid-point of $AM$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$D$ and $E$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$, so $DE \parallel BC$ (mid-point theorem); hence $DP \parallel BM$.

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle LMN$, $P$ and $Q$ are the mid-points of $LM$ and $LN$. $PQ$ is produced to $R$ so that $QR = PQ$, and $NR$ is joined.

(a) Prove that $\triangle LPQ \cong \triangle NRQ$. [3]

(b) Hence prove that $PMNR$ is a parallelogram, and deduce that $PQ \parallel MN$ and $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}MN$. [3]

(c) $LM = 11.6$ cm, $LN = 14.2$ cm and $MN = 17.4$ cm. Find the perimeter of $\triangle LPQ$ and the perimeter of the quadrilateral $PMNQ$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In $\triangle LPQ$ and $\triangle NRQ$: $LQ = QN$ ($Q$ is the mid-point of $LN$), $PQ = QR$ (construction), and $\angle LQP = \angle NQR$ (vertically opposite angles). So $\triangle LPQ \cong \triangle NRQ$ (SAS).

(b) From the congruence $NR = LP$, and $LP = PM$ ($P$ is the mid-point of $LM$), so $NR = PM$. Also $\angle QLP = \angle QNR$ (corresponding parts), and these are alternate angles for the lines $LM$ and $NR$ with transversal $LN$, so $NR \parallel LM$, that is $NR \parallel PM$. One pair of opposite sides of $PMNR$ is equal and parallel, so $PMNR$ is a parallelogram. Hence $PR \parallel MN$ and $PR = MN$. As $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}PR$, we get $PQ \parallel MN$ and $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}MN$.

(c) $LP = 5.8$ cm, $LQ = 7.1$ cm and $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 17.4 = 8.7$ cm. The perimeter of $\triangle LPQ$ is $5.8 + 7.1 + 8.7 = 21.6$ cm. For $PMNQ$: $PM = 5.8$, $MN = 17.4$, $NQ = 7.1$ and $QP = 8.7$, so its perimeter is $5.8 + 17.4 + 7.1 + 8.7 = 39$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The proof turns the two mid-points into a pair of congruent triangles; the doubled segment $PR$ then forms a parallelogram with the base $MN$. Part (c) uses the theorem for $PQ$.

(b) NR = LP = PM and NR parallel to LM (alternate angles)
(b) PMNR is a parallelogram (one pair of sides equal and parallel)
(b) PR = MN, PQ = half of PR, so PQ parallel to MN and half of it
(c) LP = 5.8, LQ = 7.1, PQ = 8.7; perimeter of LPQ = 21.6 cm

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle XYZ$, $P$ is the mid-point of $XY$ and the line through $P$ parallel to $YZ$ meets $XZ$ at $Q$. Let $Q'$ be the mid-point of $XZ$.

(a) State what the mid-point theorem tells you about $PQ'$. [3]

(b) Explain why $PQ$ and $PQ'$ must be the same line, and hence prove that $Q$ is the mid-point of $XZ$. [3]

(c) $XZ = 13.4$ cm, $YZ = 9.8$ cm and $\angle XYZ = 55^\circ$. Find $XQ$, $PQ$ and $\angle XPQ$, giving reasons. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $P$ and $Q'$ are the mid-points of $XY$ and $XZ$, so by the mid-point theorem $PQ' \parallel YZ$ and $PQ' = \dfrac{1}{2}YZ$.

(b) Through the point $P$ there is only one line parallel to $YZ$. Both $PQ$ (given) and $PQ'$ (part (a)) pass through $P$ and are parallel to $YZ$, so they are the same line. Then $Q$ and $Q'$ are both the point where this line meets $XZ$, so $Q = Q'$, and $Q$ is the mid-point of $XZ$.

(c) $XQ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 13.4 = 6.7$ cm. $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 9.8 = 4.9$ cm. Since $PQ \parallel YZ$, the corresponding angles $\angle XPQ$ and $\angle XYZ$ are equal, so $\angle XPQ = 55^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: This is the proof of the converse of the mid-point theorem: the mid-point theorem produces the line $PQ'$, and the uniqueness of the parallel through $P$ shows that it is the line $PQ$ already drawn.

marking_scheme.step: (b) only one line through P is parallel to YZ
(b) PQ and PQ-dash coincide, so Q = Q-dash
(b) Q is the mid-point of XZ
(c) angle XPQ = 55 degrees (corresponding angles, PQ parallel to YZ)

questions.stem_md:
In the quadrilateral $ABCD$, $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ are the mid-points of $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$.

(a) By joining $AC$, show that $PQ \parallel SR$ and $PQ = SR$. [3]

(b) By joining $BD$, show that $PQRS$ is a parallelogram. [3]

(c) The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ are perpendicular, with $AC = 26$ cm and $BD = 18$ cm. Name the figure $PQRS$ and find its perimeter and its area. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In $\triangle ABC$, $P$ and $Q$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $BC$, so $PQ \parallel AC$ and $PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}AC$. In $\triangle ADC$, $S$ and $R$ are the mid-points of $DA$ and $DC$, so $SR \parallel AC$ and $SR = \dfrac{1}{2}AC$. Hence $PQ \parallel SR$ and $PQ = SR$.

(b) In $\triangle BCD$, $Q$ and $R$ are the mid-points of $BC$ and $CD$, so $QR \parallel BD$ and $QR = \dfrac{1}{2}BD$. In $\triangle ABD$, $P$ and $S$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $DA$, so $PS \parallel BD$ and $PS = \dfrac{1}{2}BD$. So $QR \parallel PS$, and with part (a) both pairs of opposite sides of $PQRS$ are parallel: $PQRS$ is a parallelogram.

(c) $PQ = SR = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 26 = 13$ cm and $QR = PS = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 = 9$ cm. Since $PQ \parallel AC$, $QR \parallel BD$ and $AC \perp BD$, the sides $PQ$ and $QR$ are perpendicular: $PQRS$ is a rectangle $13$ cm by $9$ cm. Its perimeter is $2(13 + 9) = 44$ cm and its area is $13 \times 9 = 117$ cm$^{2}$.

questions.solution_md: The diagonals act as the third side of two pairs of triangles, so the mid-point theorem is used four times. In part (c) perpendicular diagonals make the parallelogram a rectangle.

marking_scheme.step: (a) PQ parallel to AC and PQ = half of AC (triangle ABC)
(a) SR parallel to AC and SR = half of AC (triangle ADC)
(a) so PQ parallel and equal to SR
(b) QR parallel to BD, QR = half of BD (triangle BCD)
(b) PS parallel to BD, PS = half of BD (triangle ABD)
(b) both pairs of opposite sides parallel: parallelogram
(c) sides 13 cm and 9 cm; rectangle (perpendicular diagonals)
(c) perimeter 44 cm and area 117 square cm

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ is the mid-point of $BC$ and $E$ is the mid-point of $AD$. $BE$ produced meets $AC$ at $F$. A line $DG$ is drawn through $D$ parallel to $BF$, meeting $AC$ at $G$.

(a) Prove that $G$ is the mid-point of $FC$. [3]

(b) Prove that $F$ is the mid-point of $AG$. [3]

(c) Hence show that $AF = \dfrac{1}{3}AC$. If $AC = 16.5$ cm and $BF = 14.8$ cm, find $AF$, $FC$ and $DG$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In $\triangle BCF$, $D$ is the mid-point of $BC$ and $DG \parallel BF$ (construction). By the converse of the mid-point theorem, $G$ is the mid-point of $FC$.

(b) In $\triangle ADG$, $E$ is the mid-point of $AD$ and $EF \parallel DG$ (as $EF$ lies along $BF$). By the converse of the mid-point theorem, $F$ is the mid-point of $AG$.

(c) From (a) and (b), $AF = FG$ and $FG = GC$, so $AF = FG = GC$ and $AF = \dfrac{1}{3}AC$. With $AC = 16.5$ cm: $AF = \dfrac{16.5}{3} = 5.5$ cm and $FC = 2 \times 5.5 = 11$ cm. In $\triangle BCF$ the mid-point theorem gives $DG = \dfrac{1}{2}BF = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 14.8 = 7.4$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The converse of the mid-point theorem is used twice, in two different triangles that share the line $AC$.

marking_scheme.step: (a) triangle BCF: D mid-point of BC and DG parallel to BF
(a) converse of the mid-point theorem: G is the mid-point of FC
(b) triangle ADG: E mid-point of AD and EF parallel to DG
(b) converse: F is the mid-point of AG
(c) AF = FG = GC, so AF = one third of AC
