questions.stem_md:
$ABCD$ is a trapezium with $AB \parallel DC$. $M$ and $N$ are the mid-points of the legs $AD$ and $BC$.

(a) The line through $M$ parallel to $AB$ meets $BC$ at $N'$. Use the equal intercept theorem to prove that $N'$ is the mid-point of $BC$, so that $N' = N$. [3]

(b) $AN$ is produced to meet $DC$ produced at $E$. Prove that $\triangle ABN \cong \triangle ECN$, and hence that $MN = \dfrac{1}{2}(AB + DC)$. [3]

(c) $AB = 16.4$ cm and $DC = 23.6$ cm. Find $MN$ and the length of the segment joining the mid-points of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The lines $AB$, $MN'$ and $DC$ are parallel, and on the transversal $AD$ they cut equal intercepts $AM = MD$. By the equal intercept theorem they cut equal intercepts on the transversal $BC$: $BN' = N'C$. So $N'$ is the mid-point of $BC$, which is $N$.

(b) In $\triangle ABN$ and $\triangle ECN$: $BN = NC$ ($N$ is the mid-point), $\angle ANB = \angle ENC$ (vertically opposite angles) and $\angle ABN = \angle ECN$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel CE$). So the triangles are congruent (ASA), giving $AN = NE$ and $CE = AB$. In $\triangle ADE$, $M$ and $N$ are the mid-points of $AD$ and $AE$, so $MN \parallel DE$ and $MN = \dfrac{1}{2}DE = \dfrac{1}{2}(DC + CE) = \dfrac{1}{2}(DC + AB)$.

(c) $MN = \dfrac{1}{2}(16.4 + 23.6) = \dfrac{40}{2} = 20$ cm. The segment joining the mid-points of the diagonals is half of the difference of the parallel sides: $\dfrac{1}{2}(23.6 - 16.4) = \dfrac{7.2}{2} = 3.6$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) is an application of the equal intercept theorem, part (b) is the proof of the mid-line formula through a congruence and the mid-point theorem, and part (c) uses the formula and its companion for the diagonals.

marking_scheme.step: (a) AB, MN-dash, DC parallel with AM = MD on AD
(a) equal intercept theorem: BN-dash = N-dash C
(a) N-dash is the mid-point of BC, so it is N
(b) triangles ABN and ECN congruent by ASA (BN = NC, vertically opposite, alternate angles)
(b) mid-point theorem in triangle ADE: MN = half of DE = half of (DC + AB)
(c) segment joining mid-points of diagonals = 3.6 cm

questions.stem_md:
Parallel lines $l$, $m$, $n$ meet a transversal at $A$, $B$, $C$ with $AB = BC$, and a second transversal at $P$, $Q$, $R$. Through $A$ a line is drawn parallel to $PR$, meeting $m$ at $S$ and $n$ at $T$.

(a) Prove that $PQ = AS$ and $QR = ST$. [3]

(b) Prove that $S$ is the mid-point of $AT$. [3]

(c) Deduce that $PQ = QR$. Five parallel lines are equally spaced along a transversal and cut off $18.8$ cm on a second transversal between the first and the last line. Find the intercept between consecutive lines on the second transversal, and the distance between the second and the fifth line. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $AP \parallel SQ$ (as $l \parallel m$) and $AS \parallel PQ$ (as $AT \parallel PR$), so $APQS$ is a parallelogram and $AS = PQ$. Also $SQ \parallel TR$ (as $m \parallel n$) and $ST \parallel QR$ (as $AT \parallel PR$), so $SQRT$ is a parallelogram and $ST = QR$.

(b) In $\triangle ACT$, $B$ is the mid-point of $AC$ (given $AB = BC$) and $BS \parallel CT$ (as $m \parallel n$). By the converse of the mid-point theorem, $S$ is the mid-point of $AT$.

(c) So $AS = ST$, and by (a) $PQ = AS = ST = QR$. For the five lines there are four equal intercepts on the second transversal: each is $\dfrac{18.8}{4} = 4.7$ cm. The second line and the fifth line are three intercepts apart: $3 \times 4.7 = 14.1$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The proof builds two parallelograms to move the intercepts $PQ$ and $QR$ onto the line $AT$, then uses the converse of the mid-point theorem to compare them.

marking_scheme.step: (a) APQS is a parallelogram (AP parallel to SQ, AS parallel to PQ), so AS = PQ
(a) SQRT is a parallelogram, so ST = QR
(b) in triangle ACT, B is the mid-point of AC
(b) converse: S is the mid-point of AT
(c) second to fifth line: 3 x 4.7 = 14.1 cm

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = AC$, and $D$, $E$, $F$ are the mid-points of $BC$, $CA$, $AB$.

(a) Prove that $AFDE$ is a rhombus. [3]

(b) $AB = AC = 13.2$ cm and $BC = 9.6$ cm. Find $DE$, $FD$, the perimeter of $AFDE$ and the perimeter of $\triangle DEF$. [3]

(c) In another triangle $PQR$, $PQ = PR = 11.6$ cm and $\angle QPR = 90^\circ$. $S$, $T$, $U$ are the mid-points of $QR$, $RP$, $PQ$. Show that $PUST$ is a square and find its area. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In $\triangle ABC$, $F$ and $D$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $BC$, so $FD \parallel AC$; $E$ and $D$ are the mid-points of $CA$ and $BC$, so $ED \parallel AB$. Both pairs of opposite sides of $AFDE$ are parallel, so it is a parallelogram. Also $AF = \dfrac{1}{2}AB = \dfrac{1}{2}AC = AE$, so two adjacent sides are equal and $AFDE$ is a rhombus.

(b) $DE = \dfrac{1}{2}AB = 6.6$ cm and $FD = \dfrac{1}{2}AC = 6.6$ cm. The perimeter of the rhombus $AFDE$ is $4 \times 6.6 = 26.4$ cm. Also $EF = \dfrac{1}{2}BC = 4.8$ cm, so the perimeter of $\triangle DEF$ is $6.6 + 6.6 + 4.8 = 18$ cm.

(c) As in (a), $PUST$ is a parallelogram with $PU = \dfrac{1}{2}PQ = 5.8$ cm and $PT = \dfrac{1}{2}PR = 5.8$ cm, so it is a rhombus. Its angle at $P$ is $\angle QPR = 90^\circ$, and a rhombus with one right angle is a square. Its area is $5.8 \times 5.8 = 33.64$ cm$^{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) uses the mid-point theorem twice and the equal sides $AB = AC$. In part (c) the same argument gives a rhombus, and the right angle at $P$ makes it a square.

marking_scheme.step: (a) FD parallel to AC and ED parallel to AB: parallelogram
(a) AF = AE (half of AB = AC): rhombus
(b) DE = FD = 6.6 cm and perimeter of AFDE = 26.4 cm
(b) EF = 4.8 cm and perimeter of DEF = 18 cm
(c) PUST is a rhombus with PU = PT = 5.8 cm
(c) angle P = 90 degrees, so a square
